lines.text: Your AI model leaks. Someone retrains it a little, so it no longer looks like yours. Can a hidden mark survive that?
You could hide one big mark in one place. But a big mark is easy to find, easy to cut out, and it can hurt the model.
lines.source: old lab film, scene 2 (one large mark is conspicuous and can hurt accuracy)

lines.text: So spread it thin: a nudge so small, across so many of the model's numbers, that no single one looks unusual.
lines.source: scene 3 (a small shift along a secret pattern across many weights)

lines.text: To read it back, line every nudge up against your secret pattern, and add them together. The pattern adds up. The noise points every which way, and mostly cancels.
lines.source: scene 3 (matched filter: the aligned marks add coherently, independent noise adds in quadrature)

lines.text: What comes out is a single score. An innocent model lands near zero. A marked one lands far away. You draw a line between them, knowing how rarely chance would cross it.
lines.source: scene 4 (a one-sided Z-test: N(0,1) for an innocent model, N(d,1) for a marked one; the threshold sets the false-alarm rate)

lines.text: And the wider you spread the mark, the further apart the two land, while every nudge stays tiny.
lines.source: scene 5 (effect size d grows as the square root of the number of marked weights)

lines.text: A thief who shakes the weights to hide it can only move the score by as much as they shake. That is a limit on this test. It doesn't promise that no mark can ever be removed.
lines.source: scene 6 (a perturbation of bounded norm moves the score by at most that norm; not a universal claim)

lines.text: And it rests on assumptions: random noise, and a clean copy of your pattern. Break them, and the advantage shrinks.
lines.source: scene 5, appendix (assumptions: independent noise, a clean reference)

lines.text: A whisper, repeated across a million numbers, can be heard over the noise. In our research, we pair a mark like this with a record of the training itself.
lines.source: the author's view; Ural and Yoshigoe, IEEE Access 2024
